claims.text: The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is equiatomic, corresponding to approximately 25 at.% of each element.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy has high chemical short-range order.
The initial FeNiCrMn alloy has severe local lattice distortion.
The initial material is free of pre-existing vacancy clusters and secondary phases.
Plastic deformation is mediated by 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations that create intrinsic stacking faults on {111} planes.
Partial-dislocation density increases monotonically with strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Macroscopic yield stress remains relatively insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Lattice friction arising from constituent atomic-size or lattice-parameter mismatch dominates the yielding response.
Dislocation nucleation occurs by thermal activation over a Peierls barrier modulated by local lattice distortion.
Vacancy clusters do not govern dislocation nucleation.
Loading along <11-1> requires a higher applied stress than loading along <110> to activate the primary Shockley-partial slip system.
The maximum yield stress for the <11-1> orientation is 5–10% higher than for the <110> orientation.
The HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking-fault structures rather than products of a thermodynamic FCC-to-HCP phase transformation.
Low stacking-fault energy stabilizes the HCP-like intrinsic stacking-fault regions.
The HCP-like regions will have a lattice parameter c exactly 1.633 times the FCC matrix lattice parameter a.
No new diffraction peaks corresponding to a stable HCP phase will appear after deformation.
A deviation greater than 2% from the ideal 1.633 lattice-parameter ratio would identify the HCP-like region as a true phase transformation.
Pure FCC metals generally have strongly strain-rate-dependent yield strength and minimal orientation effects because of low lattice friction and high stacking-fault energy.
